canberra.title: $18 million price tag sees ACT ditch electronic monitoring despite big jump in family violence
canberra.snippet: The ACT Government has abandoned its 2024 election commitment to introduce electronic monitoring of offenders, citing an annual cost of u...
canberra.content:
The ACT Government has shelved its plans to implement electronic monitoring of violent perpetrators in the Territory citing cost pressures. Photo: yasharu.

The ACT Government has abandoned its 2024 election commitment to introduce electronic monitoring of offenders, citing an annual cost of up to $18 million, despite domestic and family violence incidents rising 33 per cent over five years.

The decision has sparked a furious response from women’s safety advocates, who accuse the government of putting budget pressures ahead of protecting victim-survivors.

The ACT remains the only Australian jurisdiction without electronic monitoring technology, commonly used through GPS-enabled ankle bracelets to track offenders in the community.

YWCA Canberra chief executive officer Frances Crimmins said the decision sent a devastating message to women experiencing violence.

“The ACT Government has put a price on women’s safety,” her organisation said in a statement.

The government’s decision comes as ACT Policing’s latest annual report reveals officers attended 4478 domestic and family violence incidents, with reported incidents increasing by 33 per cent over the past five years.

The government had promised a staged rollout of electronic monitoring, beginning with offenders on intensive correction orders, parole, limited bail and leave permits.

Later stages were expected to include home detention, early release, post-release supervision, and intensive monitoring of domestic and family violence perpetrators.

But after years of feasibility studies and consultation, the government has now ruled out implementation during the current term.

A Justice and Community Safety Directorate spokesperson said the proposed system would be expensive to establish and operate.

The feasibility study estimated annual base costs of more than $4 million to monitor a relatively small number of offenders under community corrections supervision, rising to more than $18 million for a domestic and family violence monitoring scheme. These figures exclude initial establishment costs.

The spokesperson said effective monitoring, particularly for domestic violence perpetrators, required more than simply fitting offenders with ankle bracelets.

It would need comprehensive risk assessments, responsive monitoring systems, effective supervision, information-sharing between agencies and safety planning with people at risk of further harm.

While acknowledging electronic monitoring could improve compliance with community-based orders and promote public safety, the government said competing financial priorities meant the scheme could not proceed.

Treasurer Chris Steel defended the decision, saying the government had to weigh the scheme against other spending commitments.

“It’s not a matter directly in my portfolio responsibilities, but I’ll say generally as the Treasurer that when we’re looking at the range of priorities in the budget, we do have to make sure that our decisions are affordable,” he said.

“Spending $18 million on that in the short-term wasn’t going to be a priority when there are a huge range of other priorities both in corrections and right across government.”

Mr Steel compared the annual cost to an additional 1 per cent increase in territory rates, above existing increases.

Asked whether abandoning the 2024 commitment raised questions about other election promises, he maintained the government was continuing to deliver its broader agenda.

He pointed to commitments including the new Canberra aquatic facility and investment in social infrastructure.

“That one didn’t stack up and so we weren’t going to move forward with a project that was going to cost $18 million in the short-term,” he said.

The government had allocated $377,000 over two years in its 2023–24 Budget to investigate and develop an implementation plan.

In 2024, it indicated the scheme could be introduced within months, but no implementation funding was included in the 2025–26 Budget.

Instead, remaining funds were directed towards feasibility studies and policy work.

During budget estimates, Justice and Community Safety Directorate director-general Ray Johnson acknowledged that no priority group had been selected.

“They all carry a different level of risk … there might be a greater value but [also] a greater risk in different cohorts and there might be an order of batting … on where you start,” he told the hearing.

For women’s safety advocates, the latest decision raises questions about why the government continued consulting on the scheme without ultimately committing to its introduction.

YWCA Canberra said it had participated in consultations on the proposed monitoring system in good faith, providing advice on its design and operation.

The organisation said it had warned at the time that the ACT was already well behind other jurisdictions.

Ms Crimmins criticised the government’s lack of transparency, saying it had consulted extensively with the women’s safety sector on the design and implementation of electronic monitoring, only to quietly abandon the scheme.

She said the decision was buried in a 12 June Legislative Assembly speech, with the government citing significant cost pressures and competing priorities.

YWCA Canberra said the decision was especially disappointing given the ACT Government’s participation in National Cabinet commitments to strengthen perpetrator accountability and work towards ending violence against women and children within a generation.

The organisation accused the government of prioritising financial considerations and offender outcomes over women’s safety.

canberra.title: Tweaked Digital Duty of Care bill introduced to parliament
canberra.snippet: Communications Minister Anika Wells says she will look at any further amendments to her digital duty of care bill in good faith, but want...
canberra.content:
Communications Minister Anika Wells has introduced her amended Digital Duty of Care legislation to Federal Parliament. Photo: Facebook.

Communications Minister Anika Wells says she will look at any further amendments to her digital duty of care bill in good faith, but wants to see it passed intact as much and as soon as possible.

The minister introduced the Federal Government’s legislation to the House of Representatives on Thursday (15 October), where it will face little opposition thanks to Labor’s commanding majority in the Lower House.

But the government must negotiate in the Senate for the planned changes to become law.

“I need to get this through the Senate, to legislate a baseline basic safety standard,” Ms Wells said.

Labor already amended the legislation to remove a controversial clause that would have granted the Communications Minister of the day total discretion to decide what constitutes “harmful content” on social media.

Under the changes, further inclusion of harmful definitions would now have to be legislated.

That has kept the Greens happy to some extent, but they want the legislation to go further and include a provision for individuals to seek compensation from tech companies for harmful content.

Greens communications spokesperson Sarah Hanson-Young said the party agrees with the bill’s intent, but “key elements” are still missing.

The Greens have secured a Senate inquiry into the bill, which will report back before the end of the parliamentary year.

“That is a fundamental part of any duty of care package to give it teeth, to make sure it actually can work,” she said.

“I am also concerned there is little in the legislation itself that deals with the addiction elements of algorithms and social media.”

The Coalition opposes the legislation, even after the amending clause was added.

Liberal frontbencher James Paterson described the bill as “unsalvageable” and said it should be abandoned.

“We cannot support it because ultimately, the problem here is not any one clause in the bill; it’s the government’s intent,” he said.

“They’ve lied repeatedly on negative gearing, on capital gains tax, or trusts, on superannuation, on income taxes, on so many other issues.

“It turns out, if you lie to people repeatedly, then they don’t trust you, and no social media bill is going to fix that problem for you.

“But it might censor the views of Australians in the process.”

The legislation requires big tech companies to mitigate risks of online harm by giving users an opt-out choice over the algorithms in their social media feeds.

The minister told the National Press Club Thursday afternoon that parents had valid concerns about AI chatbots and online gaming platforms.

“Online safety should not be a political issue,” Ms Wells said.

“There is no reason why we can’t work together to get this done.”

She said the bill prioritises safety by design, not safety as an afterthought.

Content that causes serious distress, including abuse and bullying, will be outlawed.

Under-18s must be protected from content and features that harm young people.

This includes content that promotes or encourages eating disorders; that glorifies crime or dangerous stunts; and pornography or content that promotes hostile ideas about women and gender equality.

“I think most people would look at that list and think that was pretty reasonable,” Ms Wells said.

“Platforms shouldn’t be inundating young boys with content that demeans women, that says consent doesn’t matter.

“Young girls should not be served an endless stream of content that glorifies eating disorders. And bullying is no longer the realm of the playground or the school bus.

“It follows kids home, gets slipped under their pillow at night and is the first thing they see when they wake up.

“Under the digital duty of care, platforms will have to do more to detect and intervene in cyberbullying.

“It’s up to them to test the brakes on the car and the bolts on the swings in the park.”

The minister likened the move on social media to making seatbelts in cars compulsory, random breath testing and plain packaging on tobacco products – all of which were resisted when introduced but are now widely regarded as sensible.

“Australians have a pretty simple attitude to problems,” she said.

“If it’s broke, fix it … Australia’s digital duty of care will set basic safety standards for the online services we use every day, just like we have in every other industry.

“We must shift the burden from the shoulders of victims to the companies that are creating the environments where harms occur.

“The core of the duty is to provide a safe online environment, where all Australians are protected from seriously harmful and illegal content…

“The problem today is that big tech has been allowed to live-test its products on Australians.

“Today I want to make one simple argument: if you build it, you are responsible for its risks.”

canberra.title: Hidden video camera found in women’s bathroom on navy survey ship
canberra.snippet: Defence has commenced an investigation after a hidden video recording device was found in a women’s shower onboard the Royal Australian N...
canberra.content:
HMAS Leeuwin was due to sail from Cairns but has remained alongside while the incident is investigated. Photo: LSIS Kayla Jackson, ADF.

Defence has commenced an investigation after a hidden video recording device was found in a women’s shower onboard the Royal Australian Navy’s HMAS Leeuwin.

The find was revealed on Wednesday (14 October) by independent senator for Tasmania Jacqui Lambie in parliament after she was reportedly tipped off in a letter about the find.

HMAS Leeuwin is a 71-metre long, 2200-tonne hydrographic survey ship based at Cairns in north Queensland, and has a crew complement of 46. The ship is one of three vessels in the class and was commissioned in 2000.

Senator Lambie, an Australian Army veteran and advocate for defence personnel and veterans, revealed the recording device had been found while the vessel was alongside at Cairns.

“The sender told me that concealed cameras have recently been found in the female sailors’ showers facilities on the vessel HMAS Leeuwin, based in Cairns,” she told the Senate.

“I was also told this had occurred recently and prevented the vessel from sailing while investigations were ongoing.

“Even more disturbing are claims that footage from these cameras may have been uploaded online before the cameras were discovered,” she added.

“How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent? These are the questions today I ask Navy.”

On Wednesday afternoon Defence released a statement confirming the find, and that the incident had been referred to the Joint Military Police Unit which is working with civilian authorities.

“On 11 October 2026, Defence became aware that a video recording device had been located in the cabin of Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin, while alongside in Cairns, Queensland,” it said.

“Defence takes this incident extremely seriously and does not tolerate unacceptable behaviour in any form.

“The ship remained alongside to enable the investigation and ensure immediate support was provided to members of the ship’s crew,” it added.

“The welfare of individuals remains Defence’s priority, and support is ongoing.

“As the matter is currently under investigation and to protect the privacy of the affected individuals, Defence is unable to provide further comment at this time.”

When asked about Defence’s response to the incident, Senator Lambie responded, “What I want to know is, have they gone around on the rest of those boats, the subs, whatever, and had a look and make sure there’s no other cameras?”

“Because we are not sure whether it’s coming from contractors that go on them, or whether it’s come from Defence members,” she said.

“Defence needs to know this – your people had a gutful.

“And if there was abuse going on, they’re now coming to me, OK? I’m right on their tail, enough is enough, get control of what is going on in the Defence Force.

“Enough is enough. Don’t enlist until it’s fixed. I cannot stress that enough. Do not let your kids in there, and certainly do not let your daughters or granddaughters enlist until it’s fixed.”

The ABC reported that Greens leader and defence spokesman David Shoebridge had described the incident as “incredibly concerning”.

“We know many women aren’t feeling safe inside Defence spaces, and again we say to Labor, you’ve got to restore faith with Defence personnel, you’ve got to make women and other people feel safe in Defence spaces.”

Defence advises that professional support is available to its people at any time on one of the following support lines:

  • Sexual Misconduct Prevention and Response Office (SeMPRO) – 1800 SEMPRO (1800 736 776) (24/7)
  • Defence All-hours Support Line (ASL) – 1800 628 036 (24/7)
  • Defence Member and Family Helpline – 1800 624 608 (24/7)
  • 1800 IMSICK – 1800 467 425 (24/7)
  • Reserve Assistance Program (RAP) – 1300 687 327
  • Employee Assistance Program – 1300 687 327 (For APS, ASD, ASA, Reservists and Cadets)
  • Defence Chaplaincy Support – 1300 333 362 (24/7)

Original Article published by Andrew McLaughlin on PS News.

canberra.title: WATCH: Car chase ends when allegedly stolen car crashes into parked ute, police say
canberra.snippet: Police chased an allegedly stolen car through Belconnen before its driver crashed into another vehicle that was parked at a building site...
canberra.content:
15 October 2026

15 October 2026

Police say the car chase ended when the driver crashed into a stationary ute at a building site. Photo: ACT Policing.

Police chased an allegedly stolen car through Belconnen before its driver crashed into another vehicle that was parked at a building site.

An ACT Policing spokesperson said a Toyota Camry was allegedly stolen from the Tuggeranong pool carpark on Wednesday morning (14 October).

Police spotted it in Dickson around midday and followed it to Kaleen.

When officers tried to stop the car, its driver allegedly fled, even though police deployed stop-sticks.

The car crossed a greenbelt in Kaleen before police again deployed stop-sticks. When they did, the driver allegedly swerved towards a police officer.

“The car continued to fail to stop for police before it collided with a stationary utility at a residential building site,” the police spokesperson said.

Footage shows a witness running over and banging on the stolen car’s window after the crash, before the driver was pulled from the vehicle.

The 43-year-old man alleged to have been driving the Camry was charged with driving at police, failing to stop for police, driving a motor vehicle without consent, taking a motor vehicle without consent and dangerous driving.

He faced the ACT Magistrates Court on Thursday (15 October).

australia.title: Woman charged after allegedly poisoning colleague’s curry lunch with snail pellets
australia.snippet: Western Australian police say woman ‘experienced numbness to her tongue’ after tasting the curry at her workplace in Perth Get our breaki...
australia.content:
A woman has been charged after allegedly poisoning a co-worker’s lunch curry with snail pellets.

Western Australian police say a 58-year-old woman brought a container of curry to share with colleagues at her workplace in Perth’s southern suburbs in February.

A 43-year-old woman allegedly contaminated it with snail pellets containing metaldehyde, a poisonous substance, a police spokesperson said on Thursday.

“The curry had been shared among employees and consumed without issue during a morning tea break,” police said.

“After the meal, the accused accessed a chemical storage shed and later entered the staff lunch room where the food was kept.”

At lunchtime, the alleged victim went to eat some more of her curry.

When she opened the container, she spotted bright green granules in the food.

“After tasting a small amount, (she) experienced numbness to her tongue,” the police spokesperson said.

It will be alleged the accused and the victim were in a personal relationship.

Detectives arrested the 43-year-old woman last week.

She has been charged with one count of unlawful act or omission with intent to harm (endangering the life, health or safety of any person).

She is scheduled to appear before Armadale magistrates court on 5 November.

Police declined to provide further information about the relationship or the workplace.

australia.title: ADF member ‘person of interest’ after video recorder found in HMAS Leeuwin women’s showers
australia.snippet: Vice Adm Buckley calls incident an ‘act of sexual violence’ and a ‘despicable betrayal of trust’ Get our breaking news email , free app o...
australia.content:
The defence department says a member of the Australian Defence Force is a “person of interest” in investigations after a video recording device was found in a bathroom on HMAS Leeuwin, in what the chief of navy called a “despicable betrayal of trust”.

A day after senator Jacqui Lambie told the Senate that a hidden camera had been found in a female shower facility onboard the naval ship, docked in Cairns, navy chief Matt Buckley confirmed a “video recording device” had been located in one of the ship’s bathrooms.

In a statement, Vice Adm Buckley called the incident an “act of sexual violence” and “the most despicable betrayal of trust”, and said the navy was conducting a review of all bathrooms across the service.

Defence confirmed on Wednesday that a “video recording device” was found in the cabin of the vessel, which it had referred to the Joint Military Police Unit. It came hours after Lambie – an ADF veteran and advocate for defence personnel – told the Senate she’d been contacted by a former member of the navy with allegations about a camera being found aboard HMAS Leeuwin.

Defence did not initially confirm where the device had been found, or any details about its investigation.

On Thursday, the department gave a further update.

“An Australian Defence Force member has been identified as a person of interest in the investigation into a video recording device being located on Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin,” the department said.

“This person is now assisting the Joint Military Police Unit with its enquiries. Navy’s focus and priority is providing support to those who are impacted by this incident.”

In a written statement, Buckley informed navy members of the update.

“I consider this a most serious matter, and accordingly, the Ship’s program has been altered to enable a rapid and rigorous investigation by the Joint Military Policing Unit,” he wrote.

“My highest priority, as always, is the wellbeing of our people.”

Buckley said the navy was conducting a “100% audit of all of our bathrooms across the Fleet”.

“This act is the most despicable betrayal of trust and is fundamentally misaligned with our values,” he said.

“You have my assurance and commitment that we will tackle this act of sexual violence with all of our energy. Any perpetrator will be held to account. Further, you should all know that eradicating sexual violence in our workplace is fundamental to the fighting efficiency of our Navy. I invite all of you to make this your priority.”

The defence minister, Richard Marles, described the incident as “reprehensible, invasive and … the most despicable breach of trust”. He said he was receiving updates on the investigation as it continued.

“There is no place for this behaviour in the Australian Defence Force. Our priority remains supporting the individuals who have been impacted,” he said in a statement on social media on Thursday.

On Wednesday, Lambie asked whether images captured by the device had been published online.

“How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent? These are the questions today I ask navy,” she said.

Buckley said “all potentially impacted personnel are receiving our strongest support”, adding that the warrant officer of the navy was in Cairns to support the ship’s company.

What we learned, Thursday 15 October

Luca Ittimani

Thanks for staying with the politics blog today. We’ll leave our live coverage there.

Here are the day’s top stories:

  • A member of the Australian Defence Force is a “person of interest” in investigations after a video recording device was found in a navy ship bathroom.

  • The navy called the incident an “act of sexual violence” and “the most despicable betrayal of trust”.

  • Jacqui Lambie said she was “not surprised” by the incident.

  • Anika Wells has said people will still be able to listen to manosphere podcasts and spread conspiracy theories under the digital duty of care laws. She rejected the Coalition claim that eSafety ‘sock puppets’ will spread disinformation.

  • The Australian Electoral Commission has warned of “emerging concern” that people are getting voting information from AI.

  • Matt Canavan has disputed the Labor trade minister’s claim he walked out of a meeting on a proposed trade deal with the European Union.

  • Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has taken leave from the party room after complaints were made, triggering an independent review.

Military police to probe bathroom camera ‘despicable breach of trust’, says deputy PM

The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, has said military police are investigating the “reprehensible, invasive” placement of a video camera which was found in the bathroom of a navy ship off the coast of Cairns.

A member of the Australian Defence Force is a “person of interest” in investigations after the video recording device was found, the department of defence has said.

The Navy chief has called the incident an “act of sexual violence” and “the most despicable betrayal of trust”.

Marles, also the defence minister, made a statement on X this afternoon. He said:

Let me be clear, the incident on board HMAS Leeuwin is reprehensible, invasive and is the most despicable breach of trust.

The Joint Military Police Unit is investigating this incident and Defence is working with civilian authorities. …

There is no place for this behaviour in the Australian Defence Force. Our priority remains supporting the individuals who have been impacted.

Pocock says interest rate rises should be replaced as companies ‘making bank’

David Pocock has urged the Reserve Bank not to raise interest rates again, calling for new tools to fight inflation.

The independent senator has told the ABC there were “a bunch” of alternatives to interest rates. He said:

We could start with something like a windfall profits tax. We’re seeing companies make absolute bank off the war in Iran, and most of those profits are flowing overseas. We could be funnelling some of that into genuine cost of living relief, anti inflationary measures when it comes to things like energy.

I think we should be looking at smarter ways, about potentially having a sliding scale for things like superannuation, where across the board, you can actually take some money out of the economy, and potentially lower it down afterwards …

We’ve got this blunt instrument [of interest rates] and it clearly just is not working at the moment.

Pocock said the RBA should not raise interest rates further as unemployment rises.

I don’t know why we keep just smashing Aussie households, raising unemployment, where clearly there are so many other factors at play.

You look at some of the big companies that paid zero tax, or, you know, 1.5% tax, while banking huge, huge revenue and profits. That’s got to end. That is also adding to inflation, but we’re not addressing it.

Greens leader will meet Ukrainian ambassador after calling for cut to military aid

The Ukrainian ambassador to Australia says he will meet the Greens leader, David Shoebridge, after Shoebridge urged the government against sending Ukraine military aid.

Vasyl Myroshnychenko said he had met Shoebridge many times and would encourage him to reconsider his view. He told the ABC:

I kind of understand and agree with [what] the Greens said, that probably militarism is a curse on modern society. I wish we would have lived in a very peaceful time and country where our borders are intact, our sovereignty is protected by international law. Unfortunately, it’s not the case for us.

Myroshnychenko said he understood other Greens members like Sarah Hanson-Young disagreed with Shoebridge.

I’ve seen a lot of pushback from the members of the party. They were surprised by this position. So I think it should be revisited.

Australian defence force member ‘person of interest’ in hidden camera on navy ship

The defence department says a member of the Australian Defence Force is a “person of interest” in investigations after a video recording device was found in the bathroom of a navy ship off Cairns.

In a blistering statement, Vice Adm Matt Buckley – the chief of navy – called the incident an “act of sexual violence” and “the most despicable betrayal of trust”. Senator Jacqui Lambie had yesterday claimed a hidden camera had been found in the female shower facility onboard the HMAS Leeuwin, and Buckley later said it had been found in a bathroom.

Defence confirmed Lambie’s claims on Wednesday, and on Thursday said in an update that its investigation had progressed.

“An Australian Defence Force member has been identified as a person of interest in the investigation into a video recording device being located on Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin,” the department said.

This person is now assisting the Joint Military Police Unit with its enquiries. Navy’s focus and priority is providing support to those who are impacted by this incident.

Hume says Coalition probably opposed to private health cuts even if pensioners exempt

The deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, says Coalition members “don’t like” any effort to cut private health rebates for older Australians, as Labor looks for a deal.

Hume has told the ABC she “absolutely” supports the expansion of aged care beds that Labor has said the reforms would pay for.

But she indicated the Coalition would not be interested in negotiations for partial exemptions, such as for people on the full pension.

We don’t like the idea that older Australians are being targeted to have their health insurance, their private health insurance rebates removed from them …

Philosophically, we want more older Australians to have private health insurance, to take the pressure off the private health, the public sector, so that all Australians can benefit from our public health system. That is older Australians paying for themselves. Now there was an incentive to do that. It was a fair incentive, but the government wants to take that away.

Hume said the government could fund the aged care reforms from other areas, like winding back the National Reconstruction fund, the Housing Australia future fund and what she described as “climate bureaucracy”, including electric vehicle subsidies.

‘On what planet are you charging for a TV?’: Butler hits out at aged care providers

The health minister has skewered aged care providers for charging residents extra fees for basic services like TV.

Guardian Australia exposed the practice in July and recent ABC reporting has found new fee structure have made the problem worse.

Mark Butler has told the ABC he discussed the issue with providers earlier this week. He said:

I’ve been going to aged care facilities regularly since the early 1990s. TVs have been there for ever. Like, on what planet are you charging an extra service fee for a TV? It has been a basic entitlement for people in aged care facilities in their rooms as long as I can remember. …

I do not consider TVs extra services. I made that really clear to them … I’m not going to sort of do a rule-in rule-out, but TVs are pretty basic … I think that [wifi] is too.

He said he had requested advice from the department and the aged care minister had sought an investigation, adding:

I said to providers, look, the new arrangements provided a level of discretion … about what could be charged for and what couldn’t be, but if providers are going to basically abuse that responsibility, we’ll have to change our approach on this.

Butler won’t rule out pensioner exemptions for private health cuts

The health minister, Mark Butler, is defending Labor’s decision to put its private health insurance reforms back to a vote after the Senate punted the bills yesterday.

Butler has spoken to the ABC about the plan to reduce rebates for over-65s with private health insurance.

He refused to directly answer when asked if the government was considering carving pensioners out of the cuts and, when asked, didn’t close the door to exempting people who are on the full pension from the reforms. He said:

Well, I’m not going to have that debate. As much as I think this is a really useful conversation, I want to have that debate in the parliament in the Senate …

Of course, we recognise the reality: we don’t have a majority in the Senate. We need a constructive debate that determines whether or not we can find a path forward that has majority support from the Senate. …

I wish I didn’t have to bring this measure to the parliament. But at the end of the day, there’s not a money tree out there to fund a huge expansion that is needed in aged care in particular.

Butler said he had been caught by surprise yesterday when the Greens supported the Coalition’s move to effectively block the bill. He said he was in contact with the Greens’ health spokesperson but was also “unfortunately … having a proxy debate” with them through the media. He said:

I hope that yesterday was a rush of blood to the head, and that now over the next several weeks, we’re going to be able to have a reasoned debate.

Luca Ittimani

Thanks Krishani Dhanji and good afternoon readers. I’ll be with you for the rest of the day.

Krishani Dhanji

Thank you all so much for joining me on the politics blog this week – I’m ready for a peppermint tea and a nap.

I’ll leave you with the brilliant Luca Ittimani for the rest of the afternoon news; there’s plenty more to come.

Shoebridge states inquiry by WA Greens will be independent

Shoebridge defers several questions, saying there needs to be a “fair and independent” inquiry.

That inquiry will be done by the WA Greens.

Shoebridge is asked if that’s really “independent” if a branch of the organisation is investigating its own.

I have confidence that there will be that degree of independence. I have confidence, that the independence is necessary for all parties to be involved. It is not my role and it would be inappropriate for me as the leader of the Australian Greens in the federal parliament to be imposing controls on that.

Asked if the party is in disarray, Shoebridge says the party has been united and effective in the Senate this sitting week.

australia.title: Victoria to become first state to make abortions free as Coalition matches Labor election promise
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Out-of-pocket costs for abortion care to be covered regardless of who wins November election as Jess Wilson says Liberals and ...
australia.content:
Victoria will become the first state in Australia to make access to abortion care free, no matter who wins the November election, with the Coalition matching Labor’s promise just hours after it was announced as it attempts to neutralise the issue.

The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, on Thursday afternoon told Guardian Australia a Liberal National Coalition government would match Labor’s commitment to cover out-of-pocket costs for abortion care up to 16 weeks’ gestation. This would include GP and specialist consultations, scans, tests or medication, which can quickly add up to more than $1,000.

The commitment means Victoria will become the first state in Australia to offer free universal access to abortion services, following the Australian Capital Territory which began covering out-of-pocket costs in 2023.

The Coalition would also expand the Victorian patient transport assistance scheme so that women in regional Victoria who must travel long distances for abortion care would also be eligible for subsidised travel and accommodation.

“The Liberals and Nationals will not allow Labor to play politics on this issue,” Wilson said.

“Labor has had 12 years to improve access to healthcare but are instead choosing to play politics.”

However, the Victorian opposition would not match Labor’s commitment to extend access to medical abortion from nine to 10 weeks’ gestation or its plan to commission a clinical review into whether it could safely be offered at up to 12 weeks’ gestation.

Currently, medical abortion is subsidised through the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for use up to nine weeks but the World Health Organization’s guidance allows for up to 12.

“Only Labor will protect a woman’s right to choose,” Labor’s health minister, Ingrid Stitt, said when she announced the election commitment on Thursday morning.

Stitt’s statement suggested that One Nation could use abortion as a negotiating chip with the Coalition in the event of a hung parliament. It read: “Polling shows the Liberals and One Nation can only form a government together. And One Nation wants to make abortion a criminal offence.”

Wilson on Thursday again ruled out changes to abortion laws under a Coalition government.

“Victorians know where I stand on this issue. There will be no changes to abortion laws under a government I lead. Full stop. And I think it’s incredibly disappointing to see Labor playing politics with women’s reproductive rights five minutes before an election,” she said.

Wilson has previously described abortion as a personal decision that should be made by women in consultation with healthcare professionals.

The premier, Ben Carroll, earlier on Thursday said Labor “decriminalised abortion and we will stand up for it” as he warned that One Nation posed a threat.

“Let’s be very clear: you’ve seen the leader of One Nation very clearly say that he wants to roll back access to abortion. He wants to rob women of their right to choose their own future,” Carroll told reporters.

Animal Justice party MP Georgie Purcell, who alongside Legalise Cannabis MP Rachel Payne has pushed for abortion care to be made free, including in a report released last year, welcomed Wilson’s commitment.

“I am grateful that Jess met the moment with grace and eased the anxiety of women across the state. The Liberals ensuring we will get the abortion care we deserve was not on my election bingo card,” Purcell said.

She said that given Labor still had “access to the public purse right now” and had the Coalition’s support, they should implement the policy immediately.

Abortion was decriminalised in Victoria in 2008, with women able to obtain a termination during the first 24 weeks of pregnancy, and later if they obtain the agreement of two doctors.

australia.title: Doctors treating Elizabeth Struhs recommended involuntary mental health assessment of her mother, coroner hears
australia.snippet: Inquest into death of Queensland girl denied insulin by her religious parents is told Kerrie Struhs believed God would heal her daughter ...
australia.content:
Doctors were so concerned about the religious beliefs of Elizabeth Struhs’ mother they recommended she be subjected to an involuntary mental health assessment because she delusionally believed her daughter would be healed from type 1 diabetes, a coroner has heard.

Child safety officers, nonetheless, decided to return the eight-year-old home to live with her mother, Kerrie Struhs, over the objections of Brisbane-based doctors, in 2019.

Elizabeth died on 7 January 2022, at her home in Rangeville, Toowoomba, after her insulin was stopped by her father, Jason Struhs. A long-term sceptic of his wife’s beliefs, he had converted to them and joined her religious sect – which subscribed to an extreme form of Christianity and denied the use of medicine – in 2021.

The coroner, Ainslie Kirkegaard, heard evidence from three child safety officers involved in Elizabeth’s case on Thursday.

Elizabeth came to the attention of the department of child safety in 2019 after she was hospitalised with late-stage diabetic ketoacidosis on 17 July, a potentially fatal ailment that affects people with type 1 diabetes who are not given insulin. The court has heard she was so unwell she was in a coma and nearly died.

Despite her poor condition, Kerrie objected to Jason driving her to hospital, believing Elizabeth would be miraculously healed.

Kerrie later participated in an interview involving child safety officers and health staff.

Contemporaneous notes taken from the meeting presented in court read: “Kerrie stated that Elizabeth cannot keep this disease and she will be healed.

“(A health) consultant stated that they have treated 100s of children and parents and no one has ever reverted back from the diabetes or got rid of type 1,” the notes read.

“Kerrie stated that she has to trust in God to heal Elizabeth as God promised her he will hear her.”

A consultant asked Kerrie what she would do if she was home with Elizabeth and her sugar levels dropped, a sign of health risk.

“Kerrie stated that she will pray straight away,” the notes read.

The coroner has heard that doctors based in Brisbane repeatedly urged child safety officers not to return her home due to her religious beliefs, which they deemed “delusional”, but one told the court on Monday she felt “stonewalled” by them.

Notes of a phone call she made at the time were presented in court on Thursday.

“Child safety officer explained that the mother would not engage in any mental health assessments if recommended given her beliefs,” a child safety officer told her.

“(The doctor) stated that this is why they believe she requires an involuntary assessment and that child safety could arrange this.”

Both parents were later convicted of failing to provide the necessities of life as a result of delaying seeking medical help during the incident, with Kerrie jailed.

Child safety officers decided to return her home into the care of her father, which they did in August.

They developed a safety plan for Elizabeth and had her parents sign an intervention with parental agreement – a form of voluntary arrangement to keep a child safe at home without needing a court-ordered custody or guardianship arrangement.

The document, which was presented in court, laid out the expectations the department had for Elizabeth’s parents.

It said child safety was “worried” that Kerrie and her other children would convince Elizabeth that she was “healed by God … which could lead to Elizabeth refusing to take her medication making her very sick or putting her at risk of death”.

Jason promised to provide insulin to his daughter and did so for two years, before he was convinced to stop by other members of the sect – known as the Saints – in 2021.

All 14 adult members of the sect were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including the group leader, Brendan Stevens.

None of the witnesses can be identified for legal reasons.

The inquest continues.

world.title: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested
world.snippet: At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports Mass arrests, forced ...
world.content:
Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report.

More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.

The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years.

The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations.

Larissa Kojoué, LGBTQ+ rights researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “LGBTQ+ people are being forced to curb their normal activities … for fear of arrest and increased stigma. Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.”

Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Senegal in 1965, but hostility towards LGBTQ+ individuals has grown in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, who ended up winning the election, and the former prime minister Ousmane Sonko promised to strengthen laws criminalising same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority.

Arrests of men and women have happened all over the country. The police say they have arrested people based on information extracted from seized phones, third-party allegations or raids on private premises.

The changes to the penal code have had a chilling effect on lawyers, who said they were afraid to represent people for fear of being prosecuted themselves, according to the report. Doctors told Human Rights Watch that the changes were discouraging people from seeking HIV testing and treatment.

While there was a 49% fall in new HIV infections in western and central Africa from 2010 to 2022, sub-Saharan Africa remains disproportionately affected by the virus, with 64% of all people living with HIV globally.

Sylvie Beaumont, a consultant with HIV Justice Network, said she had received anecdotal evidence that HIV clinics had seen a drop in attendance. “Obviously this is not good for the HIV response because people are going without treatment, they’re not going to get tested,” she said.

“The consequences are really bad and it’s sad because Senegal was a country that was doing well with their HIV response. They are shooting themselves in the foot.”

She said while the law criminalising deliberate HIV transmission was not part of the reforms to the penal code this year, there had been an “unprecedented” rate of arrests in recent months. She labelled the charges “nonsensical” because it was reported that most people had either only discovered their status upon arrest; were arrested with condoms; or were on treatment that renders transmission of the virus impossible.

The report said police had breached confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBTQ+ people by leaking details to the media, which reported personal and confidential information, including HIV status – exposing individuals to social stigma, family rejection, threats and violence.

LGBTQ+ people interviewed by Human Rights Watch said the crackdown was instilling fear among their community, and causing them to feel anxious and depressed. Many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements or relocated; some have left the country.

The report pointed out that the crackdown flew in the face of domestic and international laws that guaranteed the right to a fair trial, privacy and non-discrimination.

The changes to Senegal’s penal code is part of a trend across sub-Saharan Africa towards more punitive legislation directed against LGBTQ+ people.

There have been dozens of arrests in Niger since it criminalised “sexual relations with a person of the same sex” in February. It was the first time in the country’s history that homosexuality had been criminalised, and followed the introduction of similar laws and penal codes in neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso within the past two years. All three are ruled by military juntas.

In May, Ghana, which already outlaws gay sex, passed legislation criminalising LGBTQ+ “activities”. The bill, which has not been signed into law by the president, is the latest iteration of legislation first proposed in 2021. In 2023, Uganda’s Anti-Homosexuality Act made homosexual acts punishable by death.

world.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story
world.snippet: Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers The Zimbabwean ...
world.content:
The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”

Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho.

Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”.

She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.”

Kundizeza responded in a statement on X: “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work.

“I look forward to continuing to work with the Caine prize team, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.”

Similar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir won the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prize with The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing.

Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) was removed from the longlist of France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.

The Caine prize said in a statement that it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.”

Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself.

Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly.

“I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.”

Vara said in her article, and repeated in an interview with Front Row, that she had read a 2021 story by Kundizeza that was tonally and stylistically different from The Blue Fighter.

In his statement, he responded: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.”

Vara pointed to Pangram’s own research that found that false positives were rare, including for non-native English speakers writing in English, as well as a peer-reviewed journal article that found Pangram had “strong accuracy” when assessing mock academic papers created fully, partly or with no AI. However, she acknowledged to the BBC that there was “relatively little third-party research” on the accuracy of AI detection software.

world.title: Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns
world.snippet: Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr Guinea-Bissau has not approve...
world.content:
Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.

The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.

Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week.

But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at a press briefing, where he referred to the study as “tests”.

“The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study.

“Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, ‌must ⁠strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said.

He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV).

The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have been called into question in the past year.

The claims made in nearly all of their papers are “highly misleading”, said Charlotte Strøm, a Danish researcher who has co-authored research showing that Aaby, Stabell Benn, and their co-authors had no significant findings in 24 out of 25 studies and that they’ve chosen not to publish research that may not support their viewpoints.

“When researchers operate like this and abandon proper methodological rigor, they literally decide on the results themselves, and that is not science,” Strøm said, calling it “problematic, questionable [and] unethical”.

She added: “I believe there is serious cause for concern.”

Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight”.

Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark.

In Denmark, infants born to hepatitis B-negative parents do not receive the shot, there is widespread testing for and low incidence of the virus, and the robust healthcare system can track health outcomes and provide timely and comprehensive medical care – making it an ideal location for such a study.

“It’s completely unethical that this trial is even proposed,” because a safe and effective vaccine has been available for decades, said BK Titanji, a researcher at Emory University.

It’s “reassuring” to see Guinea-Bissau pushing back on the trial, Titanji said, adding: “A study like this one needs the highest level of ethical scrutiny. You are going to be conducting a study on the most vulnerable population, which is newborn babies, in a country that is resource-constrained.”

When Titanji recently applied for approval of a collaborative study in Cameroon, she had to include extensive documentation in her application – and it was a survey, not medical research on human subjects, she said. “I can’t come to Emory’s [institutional review board] and just be like: ‘I got permission from Cameroon.’ I have to provide the document.”

The researchers should release these documents and an updated protocol showing how the study would be conducted, she said.

Experts have decried the African experiment as “horribly unethical and cruel”, “neocolonialist” and “damaging”.

“For the government of Guinea-Bissau to stand up against the United States and Denmark exploiting its children is no small statement,” said Colette Delawalla, a researcher and founder and CEO of the non-profit Stand Up for Science. “We absolutely must respect their sovereignty as a nation.”

It would cost approximately $13,200 to buy enough vaccines through Unicef and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to immunize all newborns in Guinea-Bissau each year, Delawalla pointed out.

Everyone involved should work together to ensure that every baby in Guinea-Bissau receives the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccination, she added. “This is not muddy water: we can use Black babies to further pseudoscience or we can save children’s lives with a 20-cent shot.”

It is unclear whether the US plans to move forward with the study, even after reporting indicated that the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has again set aside $1.6m for funding for the trial this year, to be matched by private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.

“The ​study has ⁠not been approved,” the HHS told Reuters in a statement. The agency has not responded to the Guardian’s questions about the trial.

At least four members of the Danish committee resigned after approval for the trial was fast-tracked. The rules of the committee had to be changed because randomized controlled trials were outside of its purview. When committee members requested more information about the Guinea-Bissau approval, no further details were provided.

The study would enroll 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau, half of whom would be vaccinated at birth and half of whom would be denied the immunization for the first six weeks of life. Hepatitis B is widespread in the country, and infection in children can have serious lifelong effects.

Guinea-Bissau, which currently has a transitional military government following a coup in November, requested in January a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study. In the meantime, Nantote said at the time, it was “canceled or suspended”.

Other officials in Guinea-Bissau also pushed back on the research. “It’s not going to happen, period,” the foreign minister, João Bernardo Vieira, said in February.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has offered support in rolling out the hepatitis B vaccine at birth to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau. “WHO stands ready to support Guinea‑Bissau as it considers its way forward and in accelerating the introduction of the birth dose and strengthening implementation,” the organization said in a February statement pushing back on the trial.

world.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
world.snippet: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers A controversial research trial ...
world.content:
A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.

It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.

At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.

Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”

Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”

Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.

An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.

Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.

“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.

Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.

The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.

The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported by Rolling Stone. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.

The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.

In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.

Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.

According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.

The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.

“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.

Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.

Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.

The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.

Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.

This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”

When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.

Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

  • This article was amended on 13 October 2026. A previous version said CIDRAP first reported news that the research trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee. Rolling Stone had actually reported the news first.

world.title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
world.snippet: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza The Nobel peace...
world.content:
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.

The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.

“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.

“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.

Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.

“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”

In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.

“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.

The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.

“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.

“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”

Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.

The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes.

Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.

The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court.

The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”.

“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.

Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in South Africa, home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”

Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.

“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.

Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.

“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.

In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.

“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.

Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.

On Friday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”
